questions.title: What counts as "enforcement proceedings" under FOIA Exemption 7(A)—do ongoing criminal investigations qualify by themselves?
questions.question_body: In Farahi v. FBI, the court says that "ongoing criminal investigations count as 'proceedings'" under Exemption 7(A), citing CREW v. DOJ. I'm confused because I thought "proceedings" implied something more formal—like a filed case or a formal adjudication. How can a criminal investigation that hasn't resulted in charges be a "proceeding"? What's the threshold for when an investigation becomes a "proceeding" under Exemption 7(A)? Does the government just need to say the investigation is gathering evidence for a possible future case, as the court suggests quoting Juarez?

questions.title: How does deference to the FBI in FOIA cases work, and why is it heightened in national security contexts?
questions.question_body: The Farahi opinion says the FBI's invocation of Exemption 7 is entitled to deference because it's a law-enforcement agency, and that such deference is "particularly appropriate" for records implicating national security, citing CNSS. But I'm not sure I understand what "deference" means here practically. Is the court saying it takes the FBI's word for it that the records were compiled for law enforcement purposes? Or does it still independently verify the "nexus" requirement from Campbell v. DOJ? And what makes national security cases different—is it a constitutional separation-of-powers deference, or just practical institutional competence?

questions.title: When are ex parte declarations appropriate in FOIA litigation, and what can a plaintiff do to challenge them?
questions.question_body: In Farahi, the FBI submitted ex parte declarations under seal, and the court relied on them for both the Exemption 7(A) analysis and the segregability determination. The court says Farahi "did not oppose the district court's acceptance of ex parte declarations, so he cannot challenge the district court's reliance on them." But how could Farahi meaningfully oppose something he couldn't see? And the court acknowledges that ex parte declarations "handicap FOIA plaintiffs." What procedural options does a FOIA plaintiff have to push back on ex parte submissions when the subject matter is classified or sensitive? Is there any recourse, or is the plaintiff just stuck once the court allows them?

questions.title: How does the "reasonably segregable" requirement work under FOIA, and when can an agency withhold entire documents?
questions.question_body: The Farahi court says the FBI can withhold records in their entirety when nonexempt portions are "inextricably intertwined" with exempt portions. It also says that individual words or phrases that could be disclosed without harm are "neither here nor there" because "the focus of the FOIA is information, not simply words." I'm confused about the line between what is and isn't "reasonably segregable." If you can redact individual words or lines without revealing protected information, why isn't that segregable? And how does the court assess segregability when it can't publicly explain its reasoning—does it just take the agency's word for it based on the ex parte declaration?

questions.title: What happens when a FOIA declaration becomes stale due to the passage of time during litigation?
questions.question_body: In Farahi, the district court initially denied summary judgment without prejudice because of the "significant passage of time" since the FBI's original declaration, ordering the agency to update its assessment. The FBI then submitted a new declaration confirming that investigations were still ongoing. I'm confused about what triggers the need for an updated declaration. Is there a specific time threshold? And if the government's investigation drags on for years, can the plaintiff keep forcing the agency to submit updates? What if the investigation never formally closes but also never progresses—does Exemption 7(A) protect the records indefinitely?

questions.title: Can a terse supplemental FOIA declaration cure an earlier detailed one, or must each declaration stand alone?
questions.question_body: In Farahi, the court acknowledges that the Bender declaration, "considered in isolation, appears surprisingly terse"—it just says investigations "remain ongoing." But the court says context matters: the original Hardy declaration had detailed the investigation, and Bender's declaration was just an update. Farahi argued this was too conclusory under CREW. My question is: in FOIA Exemption 7(A) cases, does each declaration need to independently satisfy the government's burden, or can the court read a later declaration as a supplement to an earlier one? What if the earlier declaration is years old—can a one-line update really keep the burden satisfied?

questions.title: What are the requirements for category-based withholding in FOIA, and what happens if a plaintiff fails to specifically challenge the categories?
questions.question_body: The Farahi opinion mentions that agencies using category-based withholding must use categories that are "sufficiently distinct to allow a court to determine whether the specific claimed exemptions are properly applied" to each category, citing CREW. Farahi objected that the FBI's categories were overbroad, but the court said he "provided no specific explanation" and therefore forfeited his argument. What does a plaintiff need to do to properly challenge category overbreadth? Does the plaintiff need to have seen the documents to challenge the categories, or can they challenge the categories based on the agency's description alone? How specific does the objection need to be?

questions.title: How does the "pending or reasonably anticipated" standard for Exemption 7(A) differ from other FOIA exemptions that require showing concrete harm?
questions.question_body: In Farahi, the court says the government can show pending or reasonably anticipated enforcement proceedings simply by "attesting to their existence." This seems like a very low bar compared to other FOIA exemptions that seem to require more specific showings of harm. Is Exemption 7(A) unique in this regard? How does the "could reasonably be expected to interfere" standard compare to the harm showing required under, say, Exemption 7(E (which protects techniques and procedures) or Exemption 1 (national security)? And does the deference the court gives to the FBI in national security cases effectively lower the government's burden even further than the statutory text suggests?
